video_title: Taking CTAs Mainstream | Systematic Investor | Ep.421
gist: Andrew Beer argues that 60/40 was a historical accident of a 20-year bond bubble and gives CTAs' 27-year SocGen CTA Index statistics: crisis alpha in the dot-com bust, the GFC and 2022, a 16% max drawdown, ~330 bps alpha and a 0.34 net Sharpe ratio. He also covers their weaknesses (lumpiness, manager dispersion, no persistence) and argues that growing the pie requires rebranding as 'contrarian tactical alpha', liquid vehicles and an allocator-language pitch. CTAs are up ~15.9% YTD in 2026 on oil, AI-equity and short-rates trends, and Beer warns that a major bond tantrum may be building.

insights.claim: As of early October 2026 the SocGen CTA Index was up ~15.9% YTD (15.7% through September) and ~20% over the trailing 12 months, with the SG Trend Index ~15.8% YTD and the BTOP50 up 15.27% YTD, while the short-term traders index was up only ~5.8%.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Trend followers are having one of their best 12-month stretches, outpacing MSCI World (~13.4% YTD) and the S&P 500 (~15% TR).

insights.claim: Global bonds were down 3.15% YTD into October 2026 while MSCI World was up ~13.4% and the S&P 500 total return just under 15%, illustrating bonds failing as a diversifier this year.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: The 40 sleeve of a 60/40 is a drag in 2026, strengthening the case for alternative diversifiers.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer says the trailing 12 months is one of the best periods for managed futures he has seen because the industry avoided its usual 'two steps forward, two steps back' pattern of giving back gains.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Breaks the common allocator objection that CTA gains are quickly round-tripped (as in 2022 to early 2023).

insights.claim: Unlike 2022-23, when CTA portfolios were concentrated in a single macro theme (the two-year Treasury), 2026 featured competing narratives — AI-driven equity FOMO versus a crude oil spike and rising rates — that CTAs monetized sequentially.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Multi-theme regimes produce smoother CTA return paths than single-theme regimes.

insights.claim: CTA 2026 gains came in sequence: long crude oil bought in the $60s in January, long equities (notably AI-themed emerging markets) until a couple of months ago, and more recently short Treasuries/rates.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Shows where trend P&L originated; rates is the current driver into Q4.
insights.quote: basically buying oil at in the 60s in January

insights.claim: Beer's rule of thumb is that the best CTA years, like 2022, occur when three of the four asset classes (equities, bonds/rates, commodities, currencies) are trending profitably at once.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Count how many asset classes are trending to gauge CTA return potential.

insights.claim: Beer suggests the bond market may be building 'the mother of all bond market tantrums', while the oil and commodities backdrop does not look to be improving structurally.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Implies continued short-duration and long-commodity trend opportunity and further stress on 60/40.
insights.quote: we've got the mother of all bond market tantrums building

insights.claim: Beer characterizes the entire equity market as having become 'one crazy venture capital play' on AI.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Equity concentration in an AI narrative raises crisis risk, the scenario where crisis alpha pays.
insights.quote: the entire equity markets have become one crazy venture capital play

insights.claim: Beer dismisses the AI funding 'daisy chain' (circular financing among AI firms) by comparing it to Enron.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Signals skepticism about circular AI capex funding as a fragility in equity markets.
insights.quote: we used to call that Enron

insights.claim: Beer argues the 60/40 portfolio's dominance was a historical accident of the 2000s fueled by a 20-year bond bubble, during which bonds were the 'statistically perfect diversifier' to stocks.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Allocators extrapolating 2000-2020 stock-bond correlation are relying on an anomaly.
insights.quote: It was fueled by the 20-year bond bubble

insights.claim: From 2000 to 2020 the Bloomberg US Aggregate's max drawdown was under 4%, a function of central bank policy and bubbles that created a false perception of bonds as an ironclad asset.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Benchmarks built on that period understate bond risk.

insights.claim: Beer calls adding to bonds at end-2021 — after equities rose 28%, bonds yielded about zero and inflation was being discussed — 'among the worst mistakes an allocator could make', yet rebalancing rules forced exactly that at the peak of the bond bubble, with $18 trillion of negative-yielding bonds outstanding.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Mechanical rebalancing into a bubble is a structural flaw of static allocation.
insights.quote: it is among the worst mistakes an allocator could make

insights.claim: Beer asserts bonds currently offer no diversification value at a reasonable horizon, saying an investor might as well forget bonds and just own stocks for the same risk.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Strong anti-duration view from a prominent alternatives allocator.
insights.quote: the amazing thing about bonds right now is bonds have no value today

insights.claim: Investors keep bonds partly for behavioral reasons: Beer, despite a decade of bond criticism, owns bonds because he likes the regular coupon payments — 'your own money handing you money every month'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Income preference keeps bond demand sticky regardless of real return math.
insights.quote: Because I love the coupon like anybody else

insights.claim: Over 27 years, US investment-grade bonds have a +0.36 correlation to equities, REITs +0.65, the GSCI about +0.3 (after flipping from negative), gold about zero, and the CTA space slightly negative.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Most 'diversifiers' are positively correlated to equities over the full cycle; CTAs and gold are the exceptions.

insights.claim: Beer says the industry cherry-picked the 2000s and 2010s, an anomalous negative stock-bond correlation period, because it supported the 60/40 narrative.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Correlation assumptions in many CMAs are biased by sample selection.

insights.claim: Capital market assumptions suffer heavy recency bias, and when they prove wrong allocators go through 'existential crises' and make incremental tweaks rather than abandoning the framework.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Allocation shifts toward alternatives will be gradual and at the margin, not wholesale.

insights.claim: A late-1990s academic study showing commodity futures delivered equity-like returns with negative equity correlation sparked an allocation wave, but the correlation flipped positive by the mid-2000s.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Diversifier relationships embedded in models decay once they are crowded.

insights.claim: Beer observes that allocators are responding to the stock-bond correlation breakdown in different ways: seeking 'a different 40' while keeping the 60, or carving alternatives out of the 40.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: The 40 sleeve is the likely funding source for CTA allocations.

insights.claim: In the dot-com bust (~2000-2001) the S&P fell ~40%, the NASDAQ ~80% and non-US developed equities ~45%, while US Agg bonds rose ~30%, REITs 49%, gold and the GSCI rose, and the SocGen CTA Index gained 26%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: In that crisis every diversifier worked, which shaped portfolio construction for the following decade.

insights.claim: In the GFC equities fell 40-50%, bonds were roughly flat, high yield fell 22%, and both REITs and commodities — the favored diversifiers after the dot-com crash — fell about 50%, while the SocGen CTA Index rose 11%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: The prior crisis playbook failed; only CTAs repeated.

insights.claim: In 2022 equities fell ~20% but bonds also fell 15-20%, REITs ~25% and gold did not rise, while oil drove the GSCI up 20%+ and CTAs gained again.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: CTAs are the only diversifier that worked across all three major crises of the past 27 years.

insights.claim: Beer argues crisis alpha is structural rather than accidental because CTAs profit from large price moves away from consensus; he rebrands CTA as 'contrarian tactical alpha'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Frames trend as positively exposed to regime breaks, not reliant on any one asset's behavior.

insights.claim: Beer would bet on managed futures making money if equities fell 40% over the next year, while cautioning that no single diversifier is guaranteed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Clear expression of conviction in CTAs as an equity-bear hedge.
insights.quote: I would put my money on managed futures making money during that period

insights.claim: Volatility strategies did well in Volmageddon (February 2018) and COVID 2020 but disappointed in 2022 because it was a different kind of volatility, showing crisis hedges are regime-dependent.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Long-vol is not a reliable substitute for trend in inflationary or rate-driven bear markets.

themes.theme: CTA statistical profile vs. traditional assets

insights.claim: Beer estimates CTA space alpha versus the S&P 500 at about 330 bps per year over 27 years, at the high end of hedge fund strategies, driven by low correlation; bonds deliver 50-150 bps and gold ~9% (inflated by its recent run).
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: CTA returns are largely uncorrelated 'diversification bang for the buck'.

insights.claim: The SocGen CTA Index's max monthly drawdown over 27 years is 16%, versus 17% for the US Agg, 24% Global Agg, 51% S&P 500, 81% NASDAQ, 69% US REITs, 42% gold and 87.2% commodities.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Tactical position-cutting acts as capital preservation; CTA drawdowns are bond-like.

insights.claim: Individual CTA funds average ~25% max drawdown versus 16% for the index, with a range from ~13% to the high-30s among current constituents over 10 years and into the high-40s for funds dropped from the index, so drawdown control requires holding multiple managers.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Single-manager CTA allocations carry much more risk than index stats suggest.

insights.claim: The SocGen CTA Index has a Sharpe ratio of ~0.34 over 27 years (about cash +275 bps at under 10% vol), net of ~1.4% management and ~14% incentive fees, compared with ~0.4 for equities and bonds, 0.46 for REITs, 0.6 for gold and 0.15-0.2 for commodities.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: After fees CTAs match traditional asset Sharpe ratios while diversifying them.

insights.claim: Beer argues that CTAs were hamstrung by being put in the hedge fund bucket and compared to selection-biased hedge fund Sharpe ratios (for example Millennium's >2), when they should be placed in liquid ETFs and mutual funds and judged against liquid traditional assets.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Moving CTAs into the liquid-alternatives bucket changes the benchmark and the narrative.

insights.claim: CTA returns are lumpy: +13% in 2008, then about five flat years; +16% in 2014, then flat until 2021; +6% in 2021 and +20% in 2022; then below cash for three years before the 2026 rebound.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Lumpiness tempts allocators to time the space, which destroys realized returns.

insights.claim: Manager returns show wide annual dispersion (some CTAs down in 2026, others up 30-40%) and no persistence, which Beer attributes to modeling luck more than skill.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Chasing recent top performers is not a reliable path to better CTA returns; diversify across managers or replicate.

insights.claim: A private credit fund can claim a Sharpe ratio of 8-10 simply by not marking to market, which Beer cites to show how illiquid assets inflate reported risk-adjusted returns.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Treat smoothed illiquid-asset Sharpe ratios with skepticism.

themes.theme: Growing the pie: narrative & industry structure

insights.claim: Beer argues CTAs should be pitched as the tactical complement to strategic asset allocation: SAA gets portfolios 90% right, and managed futures adds the adaptive 10% that slow models cannot.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Positioning CTAs as complementary rather than competing with the allocator's core framework eases adoption.
insights.quote: you got it 90% right with strategic asset allocation

insights.claim: Beer argues the CTA pitch should use concrete trades, such as buying crude in the $60s before the war broke out, or buying gold when it broke $2,100 and riding it to $5,500, rather than academic behavioral-finance explanations.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Narrative examples resonate with allocators more than wonky theory.

insights.claim: Beer proposes industry-wide rebranding: 'trend following' sounds like arriving late to a party and 'managed futures' is opaque, and he points to LBOs becoming private equity, junk bonds becoming high yield and asset-based lending becoming private credit as precedents for 'contrarian tactical alpha'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Asset classes go mainstream once they are rebranded.

insights.claim: Beer says manager pitches that dwell on model nuances (short-term models, vol controls, stop losses, alternative markets) confuse allocators, who cannot evaluate them ex ante; a large RIA allocator told him 'the more people I talk to in this space the more confused I' become.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Technical complexity slows adoption beyond existing institutional buyers.

insights.claim: Beer says AQR's AQMAX mutual fund, launched in 2010 at ~121 bps with no incentive fee, grew to $14.3 billion in about five years, then fell ~20% over the next five as the second-worst performer, and that this single-manager concentration 'screwed up' the US managed futures space for wealth allocators.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Concentration in one star manager led to blame on the whole asset class; diversify across managers.

insights.claim: Beer recommends that single CTA managers pitch alongside a complementary peer fund, framing the pair as a better combination for diversification than either alone.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Joint pitching addresses the manager-selection and dispersion problem.

insights.claim: Beer argues growth in CTA allocations will not come from existing institutional bucket-fillers (roughly $300 billion already in the space) but from CIOs, wealth managers and RIAs who need a one-to-two sentence rationale.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: The marginal flow into CTAs is in wealth management and ETFs.

insights.claim: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen notes that investors who mistime a managed futures allocation rarely return, and that real transitions away from 60/40 often require a new generation of CIOs who are not anchored to past decisions.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
insights.so_what: Flows into alternatives may lag the evidence by years.

insights.claim: Beer says allocators already spend a lot of airtime on immaterial but narratively compelling trades (such as AI funding sources, or whether Japan is structurally interesting as an equity play), which he cites as evidence that clients value tactical stories.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: There is latent demand for tactical exposure that a CTA sleeve can systematically meet.

insights.claim: Beer warns that tactical overlays run by humans are dangerous: of ~20 US tactical signal-based managers going into the GFC, five got it right and built $10 billion businesses, while the other 15 later blew up.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Systematic tactical beats discretionary tactical as the vehicle for adaptiveness.

insights.claim: Beer predicts that AI will drastically lower the barriers to starting businesses: a firm that once needed $500k-$1M of working capital and four staff can now be run by one person and Claude, much as the late-1990s dot-com boom shifted American risk tolerance toward entrepreneurship.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of small-business formation and margin compression in service roles.
insights.quote: is now one person and claude

insights.claim: Beer's firm runs with seven people but functions like 25 thanks to AI efficiencies, versus 20-35 staff at the three asset managers he founded in the 2000s.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: AI is materially compressing operating headcount in small asset managers.

insights.claim: Beer finds it 'truly bizarre' that companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to provide AI services almost for free.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Raises a question about returns on AI capex.
insights.quote: we have people spending hundreds of billions of dollars to provide services almost for free
